title: Board Special Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board held a special meeting on October 1, 2026 to consider Resolution 55-26, directing Alliant Energy to submit a draft proposal addressing community concerns about the Hub City Wind Project by November 1st. The resolution passed, though not unanimously, signaling the board's intent to assess Alliant's willingness to negotiate without formally committing to a joint developer agreement. The meeting also included announcements about the county's upcoming budget process and a public strategic plan survey.

discussions.item: Staff presentation: Options for county engagement with Alliant Energy
discussions.body: County Administrator Lori McSkimmons presented a table of four options for the board: (1) negotiating a Joint Developer Agreement (JDA), estimated cost up to $20,000; (2) intervening in the PSC permitting process, estimated $75,000–$200,000+; (3) adopting a moratorium, cost unknown and noted as likely unenforceable on a 100-megawatt project; and (4) appealing the PSC's decision after issuance, estimated $20,000–$50,000. She noted PSC staff confirmed no intervention has ever stopped a project and that Columbia County's similar moratorium effort was sent back to committee. She emphasized options are not mutually exclusive and that the county could not file for intervention until after Alliant submits its formal PSC application, which could come as early as mid-December 2026.

discussions.item: Resolution 55-26 — Hub City Wind Project engagement with Alliant Energy
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson, who authored the resolution and chaired the alternative energy advisory committee, explained it does not commit the county to a JDA but rather asks Alliant Energy to submit a draft proposal addressing community concerns by November 1st, after which the board would evaluate next steps. Supervisor Dickinson expressed strong opposition, stating he would not vote for anything that moved toward a JDA and questioned whether Alliant would engage in good faith. Supervisor Leur raised concerns that the resolution puts the county in a reactive position and called for an energy summit to address broader regional energy policy. Supervisor Ritter, Supervisor Nath, Supervisor Rosenberg, and Supervisor Robinson defended the resolution as a proactive first step to gauge Alliant's willingness to address constituents' concerns on issues including decommissioning, setbacks, emergency response, property values, and health impacts. The resolution passed but was noted by Chair Gibbs as not unanimous.

discussions.item: Announcements: Budget process and strategic plan survey
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson announced that the county administrator's proposed budget was accepted by the Human Resources Finance Property Committee and is now the county board's budget. Key dates include: amendment submissions by October 9th, committee authorization for publication on October 12th, a public hearing on November 2nd at 3:00 p.m., and full board budget adoption on November 10th. Chair Gibbs noted the public hearing was moved to 3:00 p.m. on November 2nd to avoid conflicts with Election Day on November 3rd. McSkimmons announced that a public survey on the county's strategic plan — narrowing 20 objectives down to 10 priorities — would open October 2nd and run through October 23rd.

title: Health and Human Services Committee Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Health and Human Services Committee met and took action on a grant application for the PATH (Projects for Assistance in Transition from Homelessness) program, approving the county to move forward with applying for up to $150,000 in state funding to address homelessness among individuals with severe mental illness. The committee also received updates on a budget-neutral arrangement to provide temporary child welfare supervision support to Lincoln County, mid-year budget reports showing no concerns, and strategic plan community survey progress. The meeting was notable for its focus on a 67% increase in homelessness in Marathon County between 2022 and 2025.

discussions.body: A motion to approve the minutes was made by Supervisor Crumbs and seconded. The motion carried without opposition.

discussions.item: 5A: Authorization for Application for Funding from Wisconsin DHS PATH Program
discussions.body: Health department staff member Megan presented the PATH grant opportunity, explaining that Marathon County has seen a 67% increase in homelessness from 2022 to 2025 and that the grant would fund a case manager and one-time rental assistance targeting individuals experiencing homelessness with severe mental illness. She said the county plans to apply for approximately $150,000, with a 1-to-3 match requirement that Administrator Leonard clarified could be fulfilled through in-kind contributions like existing staff time rather than new county dollars. One supervisor asked about worst-case scenarios if only $45,000 were awarded, and Megan confirmed a reduced scope would still be viable. Supervisor Rosenberg asked about HUD's shift away from Housing First toward transitional housing, and Megan confirmed the grant aligns well with that changing landscape. Supervisor Cavelli noted that the homelessness task force had identified mental health as a key gap. The motion to authorize the application passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 6A: Strategic Plan Development Update Including Public Survey
discussions.body: Chair Boots noted the community survey would go live in October as part of strategic plan development. Supervisor Cavelli asked about expected response rates, referencing past survey efforts. Administrator Leonard and health department staff member Amanda noted that when the life report survey transitioned from paper to online, responses jumped from just under 400 to 1,792, suggesting confidence in the online format.

discussions.item: 6B: Social Service Department Support to Lincoln County for Child Welfare
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard explained that Marathon County is providing temporary child welfare supervision support to Lincoln County, which has experienced turnover in supervisory positions. Social Services Director Christa confirmed that Lincoln County has an offer out for their child welfare manager position and that the arrangement is expected to conclude by end of 2026. All Marathon County staff time, including after-hours on-call support, will be tracked through a time study and fully reimbursed by Lincoln County at no net cost to Marathon County.

discussions.item: 6C: Year-to-Date Budget Reports
discussions.body: Finance staff member Sam presented mid-year budget reports through June 2026 for the health department, veterans services, and social improvement fund, noting no concerns in any department. The health department payroll benchmark was at 46.47%, veterans services was at 92.91% of revenue budget largely due to tax levy timing, and the social improvement fund had $11.27 million in the grants fund. Sam noted a budget amendment will be needed at year-end for the four-county consortium.

discussions.item: 7A: Future Discussion Items and Announcements
discussions.body: A supervisor requested a future presentation or report on suicide awareness and prevention data, and health department staff agreed to track that through the PULSE framework. Administrator Leonard announced the 2027 budget had been delivered to HR, Finance and Property Committee and encouraged supervisors wishing to propose amendments to contact finance director Fensky, Leonard, or corporation counsel to ensure any amendment maintains the required balanced budget. He also reminded the committee of a special meeting the following day at 3 p.m. and asked members unable to attend in person to contact Chair Gibbs to arrange remote participation.

overview: The Marathon County Human Resources Finance & Property Committee met to receive and formally accept the administrator's proposed 2027 annual budget and capital improvement funding plan. County Administrator Leonard presented a status-quo-in-services budget featuring a 1-cent reduction in the tax rate while the average property tax bill rises modestly due to equalized value growth; the committee unanimously accepted the budget, which now becomes the county board's document subject to amendment. Key features include a $3.5 million allocation from North Central Healthcare revenues toward a new highway shop, continued homelessness and childcare workforce funding, and significant capital investments after a scaled-back 2026 CIP year.

discussions.item: 2027 Annual Budget presentation
discussions.body: County Administrator Leonard presented a 2027 budget he described as 'status quo' in programs and services, with the tax rate dropping 1 cent to $3.48 per $1,000 of equalized value while the average county property tax bill rises approximately $52.58 to $936.92 due to equalized value growth of 6.25%. He highlighted continued funding for homelessness emergency shelter ($150,000), childcare workforce expansion ($50,000 reduced level), a minimum revenue guarantee for Central Wisconsin Airport ($150,000 tied to a $950,000 federal air service development grant requiring local match), and $100,000 for PC replacements. He emphasized the cornerstone of the budget is a funding plan for a new highway shop using $30 million in designated highway reserves and $3.5 million in North Central Healthcare revenues routed through the capital plan, avoiding new borrowing. He also noted one-step wage advancement and a 1% scale shift for employees, budgeted 8% health insurance increase against a 6.5% renewal rate, and no new levy-funded positions. Areas of risk flagged included health insurance costs, high-cost social services placements (one Level 5 treatment foster care placement alone can exceed $595,000/year), and competitive labor market pressures.

discussions.item: 2027 Capital Improvement Project funding plan presentation
discussions.body: Deputy Administrator Holman walked through the CIP funding plan, noting total traditional CIP projects of approximately $7.175 million plus $3.5 million for the highway facility and $7 million in bituminous resurfacing. Highlights included increased sheriff's office fleet funding of $595,424 to catch up on 2026 and implement 2027 replacements, new election tabulator equipment for the county clerk, library elevator modernization, courthouse annex roof replacement, LVP (Lake View Professional Plaza) underground piping and interior updates, air handler replacement design near the jail, and an Adele Olson-area parking lot paving project timed to coincide with nearby highway work. He noted approximately $1 million in tax levy and nearly $900,000 in sales tax fund the capital plan, with six TID closures generating roughly $700,000 in additional operating levy capacity redirected to capital.

discussions.item: Department-by-department budget summary
discussions.body: Deputy Administrator Sam [last name inaudible] reviewed all county departments, noting notable changes including: the District Attorney's office restructured staffing to save roughly $20,000 while absorbing loss of discovery fee revenue from a state rate change; the Medical Examiner abolished the deputy chief medical examiner position; Social Services restructured rent calculations and indirect cost allocations; the Sheriff's office unfunded several positions and utilized jail assessment funds; North Central Healthcare submitted a flat levy request; and a new 'state special charges' budget line of just under $6,000 was established for civil mental health commitment proceedings in other counties. ADRC, CCITC, and Birth to Three were the only support agencies receiving funding increases.

discussions.item: Motion to accept the 2027 administrator's proposed budget
discussions.body: Chair Robinson outlined the remaining budget calendar and invited questions. Vice Chair P[inaudible] moved to accept the budget; Chair Gibbs seconded. No substantive discussion was recorded before the vote. The motion carried unanimously on a voice vote. Chair Robinson asked supervisors to direct questions in advance of the October 7 committee meeting and noted outstanding items including the Rib Mountain deputy contract still being finalized.

title: Village Board Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Village Board held its September 28, 2026 meeting, approving the Green Tree Trails subdivision preliminary plan (60+ one-acre lots with private wells and septic) unanimously after significant public comment and board discussion, and also approved a zoning text amendment allowing zero-lot-line (twin home) structures. The board received extensive budget previews including a $56,000 increase in state transportation aid for 2027, a proposed $39/year garbage fee increase driven by diesel fuel surcharges, and a 10-year Capital Improvement Plan with two 2027 borrowing projects: Maple Ridge Road and Bushna Park improvements.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Green Tree Trails Subdivision
discussions.body: Three residents spoke during public comment. Guy Friedel of Ruby Drive argued the village should pursue smaller lots with municipal sewer and water to double the tax base, suggesting referral to the utilities and APC committees and the use of special assessments. Marie Kramer of Highway 153 questioned the wisdom of private wells and septic given groundwater concerns and proximity to existing sewer service, saying 'we're walking backwards.' Joanne Mansel of Pine Road asked about minimum lot size and frontage requirements and stated she disagrees with more density, saying 'I think 60 homes is plenty' and that one-acre lots would be appropriate for the area.

discussions.item: Administrator Report
discussions.body: Administrator Jim Dabel announced the new Village Clerk will start October 19 and will be introduced at that time, noting strong experienced applicants. He reported FedEx ground-breaking is expected by mid-to-late November, which is significant for TID 1 revenues. He also praised DPW staff for site preparation work behind the municipal building, saving significant money, and noted budget materials in the packet are a precursor to the 2027 budget process.

discussions.item: DPW Report - Green Acres Road School Bus Turnaround
discussions.body: DPW Director Greg [last name inaudible] reported that a resident's concern about school buses not being able to turn around on Green Acres Road is being investigated; the existing turnaround used by plow and garbage trucks was found too small for school buses. He is coordinating with the school district and bus company to evaluate options, including a possible hammerhead turnaround, but noted the village does not control the bus company contract. Trustee Solheim asked for an update by the next meeting. The director also reported that the new employee parking garage is on track, with permits approved and concrete work expected to begin within a week and a half.

discussions.item: Finance Director Report - Per-Capita Spending Comparisons
discussions.body: Finance Director John Jacobs presented a detailed comparison of Kronenwetter against nine other north-central Wisconsin communities using 2024 state data. Key findings: Kronenwetter is near the bottom for per-capita spending on streets ($147/person), fire ($47/person), and police ($163/person); property taxes are the lowest at $317/person but 84% comes from residential versus 60-70% for peer communities. Jacobs emphasized the need for commercial and manufacturing diversification, noting TID 1 and TID 2 as critical tools, and that the FedEx distribution center could stop the $100,000-$120,000 annual general fund bleeding into TID 1.

discussions.item: Green Tree Trails Subdivision Preliminary Plan
discussions.body: Community Development Director Nathan Sandwick presented the preliminary plan for approximately 60+ one-acre lots with private wells and septic systems, noting unanimous planning commission approval in June. Board discussion focused on the history of the property (turned down nine times under previous developer), the decision not to extend municipal sewer and water due to costs over $1.6 million, and the compromise of one-acre lots meeting septic minimums. Concerns were raised about traffic on Nick Avenue, which will be gated as emergency access only. Trustee Mishka moved to approve, seconded by Trustee Coyle; the motion passed 7-0.

discussions.item: Text Amendment Chapter 520 - Zero Lot Line Structures
discussions.body: Sandwick presented a zoning ordinance amendment to allow twin homes (zero-lot-line structures) where duplexes are currently permitted on 20,000 square foot parcels, enabling each half to be individually owned. Trustee Lesniak moved to approve, seconded by Trustee Stowell. No notable debate was recorded; the amendment passed 7-0 on a roll call vote.

discussions.item: Budget Preview - Garbage Fees and Debt
discussions.body: Jacobs reported a $56,000 increase in state transportation aid for the 2027 budget. On garbage fees, he presented scenarios driven by diesel fuel surcharges in the Harder's contract; with diesel exceeding $6.50/gallon, the village faces a $57,000 shortfall in 2026. The planning figure recommended by APC of $6.25/gallon would raise household garbage fees from $228 to approximately $267.24 per year (a $39 increase). Administrator Dabel recommended using $6.25 as the planning factor for the budget while monitoring prices. Jacobs also outlined a debt restructuring plan to shift $863,000 in unused TID 2 bond proceeds to the capital project fund, reducing TID 2 debt and freeing resources, with the tax levy absorbing a small $12,000 increase in annual debt service.

discussions.item: 10-Year Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) - 2027 Projects
discussions.body: Jacobs presented the second review of the 10-year CIP, emphasizing only 43% of the $30 million plan relies on general obligation borrowing. For 2027, two borrowing projects are proposed: Maple Ridge Road (total ~$2.9M, with $1.2M already on hand reducing new borrowing to ~$1.7M) and Bushna Park improvements (~$25,000 from the park fund plus borrowed remainder). Board discussion touched on building security upgrades including key fob access (~$100,000 estimate) and cameras, audio-visual improvements to the meeting room, and the need for a long-range plan for municipal center maintenance. Jacobs noted the plan is a fluid document to be reviewed annually.

title: Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee
overview: The Village of Weston held a joint Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee meeting of the Village Board of Trustees and Planning Commission to review progress on a 10-year comprehensive plan update. Consultant Mark Roers of MD Roers Consulting presented survey results, stakeholder interview findings, draft vision statements, and preliminary chapter goals and initiatives covering land use, economic development, housing, transportation, and intergovernmental cooperation. The committee reached consensus on using draft vision statement 'C' for public presentation and set a public workshop for November 12, 2024, from 5 to 7 p.m.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: No speakers appeared in person or online. An emailed written comment from resident Sarah Prather regarding an indoor playground, addressed to Jennifer Higgins, Jamie Sean, Mark Roers, and Audrey Webster, was distributed to the board. President Maloney noted it would be entered into the record and included in the packet.

discussions.item: Meetings and Milestones Update
discussions.body: Consultant Mark Roers outlined the comprehensive plan update process, noting that a community survey drew nearly 700 respondents, stakeholder interviews reached 24 identified contacts with 10 completing interviews, and a young adult questionnaire targeting ages 20–35 yielded 48 responses via social media. Roers explained the plan is divided into three volumes, with Volume 2 (Vision and Directions) as the current focus, targeting a public hearing by March. The board noted that 48 young adult responses exceeded the typical weekly newsletter poll response of about 27.

discussions.item: Stakeholder Interview and Young Adult Questionnaire Results
discussions.body: Roers summarized cross-cutting themes from all input channels: safety ranked as the top community value across all age groups; residents want more retail, restaurants, and groceries; interviewees emphasized need for workforce housing, particularly entry-level single-family homes and duplexes over large apartment complexes; and intergovernmental respondents favored expanding collaborative services while keeping Weston's suburban character distinct from larger neighbors. Young adults specifically cited school quality, parks, family orientation, housing affordability, and indoor recreation as priorities.

discussions.item: Draft Vision Statement Review
discussions.body: Roers presented three vision statement options (A from 2016, B from the recent strategic plan, and C newly drafted by Roers with AI assistance). Pre-meeting homework showed C received seven votes, A received one, and B received none. Discussion focused on tweaking C: Trustee Brent Olson suggested removing the word 'thoughtfully' from 'Weston will grow thoughtfully,' with others suggesting 'intentionally' as a substitute; one reviewer had suggested removing 'and welcoming' from the opening line, which drew pushback; another suggested adding 'can' language in multiple places, which was debated. The committee reached consensus to bring a refined version of C to the November 12 public workshop.

discussions.item: Community Growth Map and Geographic Vision
discussions.body: Roers presented a generalized growth pattern map highlighting three mixed-use corridors (Scoffield Avenue, County Road X/Camp Phillips Road, and Weston Avenue) and identified a potential third interchange at Ryan Street as a priority transportation and land use initiative. Trustee or commissioner Gary Garn noted that Marathon County has a no-trucking restriction on Highway J south of Weston Avenue, which would need to be addressed for future southern industrial expansion. Extended discussion covered a potential bridge crossing north from the Caleb Drive area of Sandy Lane subdivision to improve connectivity, with staff noting the Oakclair River floodplain narrows at that point and that the northeast annexation area is known to the town chair.

discussions.item: Hyperscale Data Center Policy
discussions.body: Roers recommended a draft initiative to 'support more industrial development while restricting hyperscale projects,' defining hyperscale as typically requiring 100 or more acres. He cited the DeForest example of a 1,500-acre proposal that was rejected and noted concerns about power consumption, long construction periods, land obsolescence, and community division. Board members expressed agreement with establishing a policy and raised questions about when to address related issues such as solar fields, wind turbines, and EV chargers. Roers noted solar field incentives are diminishing and cited a 2,500-acre proposal near Cambridge. The committee appeared to support the proposed policy direction without a formal vote.

discussions.item: Housing Chapter and State Law Initiatives
discussions.body: Roers outlined new state-level tools including a pay-as-you-go TIF district specifically for residential development on lots no larger than 7,500 square feet with house size caps (1,500 sq ft single-story, 2,000 sq ft two-story), aimed at starter homes. He also noted infrastructure reimbursement mechanisms for developers and referenced the Truth in Planning law requiring communities to plan for sufficient housing land and be open to rezoning consistent with their plans. The board asked whether developer-fronted infrastructure costs could deter development; Roers said hybrid approaches are possible and that lenders are generally familiar with these structures.

discussions.item: Tax Incremental Financing — New Generation
discussions.body: Roers explained that TID No. 1, the larger of Weston's two active districts, will close at year-end, creating room to establish new, smaller, project-specific TIDs. He cited DeForest's model of seven active TIDs and described the shift toward pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) structures where developers front infrastructure costs and are reimbursed through incremental tax revenue, closing districts faster. No vote was taken.

discussions.item: Pre-Meeting Initiative Prioritization Results
discussions.body: Staff reported results of a pre-meeting homework exercise in which board and commission members ranked draft initiatives. 'Continue existing and pursue more opportunities for collaborative services' ranked first with six votes. Tied for second with five votes each were 'maintain the function and condition of Weston's roads' and 'help expand and attract retailers, restaurants, grocers, and industries in targeted sectors.' Tied for third with four votes each were 'phase growth according to utility, road, stormwater, and service capacity,' 'reinvest in older neighborhoods and housing,' and 'update Weston's five-year strategic plan.'

discussions.item: Shaping Weston's Tomorrow Public Workshop
discussions.body: The committee confirmed a public workshop titled 'Shaping Weston's Tomorrow' for November 12, 2024, from 5 to 7 p.m. Roers outlined plans for interactive small-group discussions rather than a lecture format, organized around topics such as transportation and natural resources. A board member requested a poster be created within 22 hours to publicize the event at a community event the following evening; staff confirmed they could produce one using Canva. Roers encouraged board members who attend to listen rather than actively participate in small groups.

discussions.item: Update on Kennedy Park renovation
discussions.body: Staff reported that contractors are scheduled to arrive the following week to address touch-up paint on poles, crack block and missing mortar, dugout door adjustments, sod restoration from irrigation leak repairs, and irrigation system restoration. discussions.item: Update on Muler Park master plan
discussions.body: Staff reported that following the September 3rd public input meeting, the consultant revised the concept design to add tennis and basketball courts and relocated the shelter near the pickleball/basketball/tennis area. Public feedback on the concept was largely positive with few suggested changes. Three emails were received requesting that any future playground addition be fully ADA-accessible. Staff noted playground equipment at Muler was intentionally excluded from the seven-playground replacement project due to its relative newness (installed 2007), but replacement would be planned if the master plan moves forward. A cost estimate is being prepared and will return to the committee for approval or denial. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Update on aquatic center repairs
discussions.body: Staff reported the contractor moved up their schedule and now expects to begin work at the aquatic center the week of October 5th, earlier than the previously anticipated late October window. Work includes leak detection, a valve and motor replacement, and winterization. Staff is preparing the mechanical room for the contractor's arrival. Electrical and commercial pool permits through the village are being processed. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Discussion and action on farmers market end-of-season survey
discussions.body: Staff presented revised survey questions for a second end-of-season farmers market survey, noting the first survey was issued too early in the season. The proposed survey has nine questions including an open-ended final question. Committee members discussed whether to include a vendor-specific survey; staff noted the existing survey already asks respondents to identify as vendors. A committee member suggested adding a 10th question asking how respondents otherwise use Kennedy Park, which received broad support. Trustee Beck, participating online, supported conducting the survey now while the season is fresh. The committee voted to proceed with the survey, to be released around October 1st and run approximately 30 days.

discussions.item: Discussion on collecting feedback regarding ice skating rinks at Kennedy Park
discussions.body: Staff recapped discussions from March and April about the cost and usage of the Kennedy Park outdoor ice rink, noting that since the warming house closed in 2019, attendance tracking has been limited but staff observe regular use. Cost to maintain the rink is primarily utilities—approximately $800 in water usage annually—since labor costs remain fixed regardless. Committee members debated whether a public survey would be useful, with concern that respondents without context might vote against a low-cost community amenity. One member noted the rink is the only full-size outdoor hockey rink (200x85 feet) in the area. The committee reached a consensus not to conduct a standalone ice rink survey, but agreed to add a question about Kennedy Park usage to the existing farmers market survey. No formal vote was taken on the ice rink item.

discussions.item: Discussion and action on completing an updated aquatic center evaluation
discussions.body: Staff noted the last aquatic center evaluation was completed in 2016 at just under $7,000, and that significant capital expenditures have followed, including over $102,000 in leak repairs this year and another motor and valve replacement project exceeding $100,000. Staff estimated a new evaluation could cost $7,000–$12,000. A committee member raised the question of whether to wait given ongoing discussions about a possible pool partnership with the Everest School District, which recently mailed a facilities survey to residents. After discussion, the committee agreed that an evaluation could actually inform the partnership decision. A motion was made and seconded to proceed with the aquatic center evaluation; the motion was approved unanimously on a voice vote.

overview: The Wausau Police & Fire Commission met on September 28, 2026, conducting organizational business including electing a new vice president and secretary after Commissioner Tom Garver's departure from the commission. The meeting featured substantive updates from Fire Deputy Chief Justin and Police Chief Barnes covering apprenticeship hiring, budget constraints, the proposed UW campus acquisition, and the department's Flock license plate recognition camera system.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Tom Garver Farewell
discussions.body: Outgoing Commissioner Tom Garver, of 4620 Huntington Court, addressed the commission to mark his departure, citing 'circumstances beyond our control' requiring him to leave. He praised the commission's culture of hiring for character, commended department leadership, and expressed confidence in newly appointed commissioners. The chair noted Garver was recently inducted into the Army Sports Hall of Fame in September for his hockey career at West Point, where he holds the program's all-time wins record with 75 victories.

discussions.item: Election of Commission Vice President
discussions.body: With Garver's departure creating a vacancy in the vice president role, Commissioner Lisa nominated Veta Perkins (referred to as 'V') for vice president. Another commissioner moved to close nominations, and the motion to elect Perkins as VP passed unanimously. The chair also appointed Lisa as commission secretary without a formal vote, stating it was an appointment rather than an election.

discussions.body: The chair asked for corrections to the August 24 minutes. None were raised. A motion to approve was made and seconded, passing unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: Fire Department Monthly Update
discussions.body: Fire Deputy Chief Justin reported nine new apprentices starting that day from a pool of 45 applicants, calling the field strong. He noted six current vacancies in the department; seven candidates were interviewed for firefighter-paramedic positions but only two will advance to the PFC for approval, leaving four vacancies remaining. He also highlighted new scheduling software intended to reduce administrative burden on battalion chiefs and reduce mandatory overtime, new training software in development, a successful DEA audit of the department's controlled substances practices led by Division Chief Matt Tormolan, and the widely publicized rescue of two occupants of a small aircraft that made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau after dark, one of whom was later identified as a gubernatorial candidate.

discussions.item: Police Department Monthly Update
discussions.body: Chief Barnes reported that a recent police hiring process drew 40 applicants after targeted social media advertising in Wisconsin, and described the preliminary interview pool as the best the department has seen. He said the department anticipates hiring eight or nine officers in the next 12 months due to three current openings and five or six expected retirements. On budget, Barnes said the department is leaving two positions unfilled through August to meet required savings, and that the overall authorized FTE count is dropping from 81 to 80 in 2027 as foundation funding for one of two downtown homeless outreach officer positions expires — the city will fund one position and the other will simply not be backfilled. Barnes also updated the commission on the city's proposal to acquire the UW-Wausau campus, noting the city is seeking six months for due diligence and has requested a $50,000 budget modification for expert consultants; a first council vote failed due to lack of quorum and one abstention, but the finance committee has since approved the modification and it will return to the full council. Barnes addressed the Flock license plate recognition camera system, stating the department owns 20 cameras at $50,000 per year on a five-year contract, that Flock does not sell city data, and that data is deleted after 30 days; a formal presentation to the PFC is planned for October or November.

discussions.item: Deputy Chief Promotional Process
discussions.body: Chief Barnes outlined the timeline for selecting a new deputy chief: letters of interest and resumes were due October 2nd, officer listening sessions with the commission (without Barnes or Fire Chief Todd present) are planned for mid-October, candidate written assignments and interviews with Barnes are set for November 11th, and PFC interviews and a vote are planned for mid-to-late November with a January 17th promotional date. Commissioners discussed whether the PFC interviews could be held during the regular November 23rd meeting; Barnes said it was feasible but noted interviews could take several hours and might require a reduced agenda.

He praised department leadership, emphasized the importance of hiring for character, and thanked his fellow commissioners.

title: Finance Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee met on September 22, 2026, and took action on several significant items including approving a budget modification for the 700 Grand Avenue apartment development (2-1), recommending the city fully fund lead service line replacements for the remainder of the program, and advancing a feasibility study for converting the W. Stevens Point campus into a public safety building. The committee also tabled a proposed increase to dog and cat licensing fees pending more information from Marathon County, and voted to enter closed session to discuss a potential purchase of county highway department property.

discussions.item: Public Comment — Pet Licensing Fees
discussions.body: Jamie Hoover, 4023 Brierwood, Wausau, addressed the committee opposing the proposed increase to dog and cat license fees. Hoover argued the 66.67% proposed increase for spayed/neutered animals was excessive, compared Wausau's proposed $25 fee unfavorably to larger cities like Appleton ($6), Milwaukee ($12), and Oshkosh ($5), and noted Marathon County does not charge for cat licenses while Wausau does. Hoover also raised broader concerns about cumulative fee increases on residents including the wheel tax, water costs, and storm water fees, and warned that higher fees would discourage licensing compliance.

discussions.item: 700 Grand Avenue Development Agreement and Tax Increment Grant — Multi-Year Budget Modification
discussions.body: Patrick presented the budget modification for the apartment project at Grand Avenue and Thomas Street, noting the project was nearing completion ahead of the anticipated December 31, 2026 deadline, with certificate of occupancy expected the same day or next. Alder Tierney objected to approving the budget modification before final paperwork and invoices were in hand, comparing it to closing on a house without documents, and suggested waiting two weeks. Staff clarified the action was only a budget modification — not authorizing a payment — and that the city would not cut a check until all compliance documentation was verified. Tierney maintained her objection; the motion passed 2-1 with Tierney opposed.

discussions.item: Budget Amendment for W. Stevens Point Campus — Public Safety Building Feasibility Study
discussions.body: Chief Barnes presented a $50,000 budget amendment for feasibility studies to evaluate converting the W. Stevens Point campus into a combined police and fire public safety facility. He explained the item had previously failed at Common Council 6-1 with one abstention and three absences, in part because a member's abstention functionally counted as a no with only eight members present. Barnes noted the city's proposal to Marathon County for the RFP process was generating interest, with meetings held with County Administrator Lance Leonard, and that the $50,000 would cover architectural and engineering studies, including quotes of $25,000 from FJMA Architects and $15,000 from Five Bugles. Alder Watson expressed support for proceeding with due diligence, and the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Lead Service Line Replacement — Options for Private-Side Costs
discussions.body: Community Infrastructure Partners (CIP) presented a detailed financial overview showing Wausau has replaced over 3,500 lead service lines and is the top per-capita replacer in the nation. Presenters warned that construction costs have risen 56% over two years and recommended completing the remaining 2,800–2,900 lines by 2028 to lock in quarter-percent interest loans and principal forgiveness grants, potentially saving $17–$37 million versus waiting until the 2037 EPA deadline. Three options were presented: Option A (city covers to 75% of cost, homeowners pay gap), Option B (flat $1,000 homeowner charge), and Option C (city covers all). Alder Watson moved for Option C — city covers full cost for the remainder of the program — citing equity concerns and the low interest rate available. Alder Tierney agreed, noting it was unfair to charge residents based on neighborhood. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Procurement Policy Amendment — Suspension and Debarment Verification
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne explained that the city received audit findings in 2023 and 2024 for failing to properly document suspension and debarment checks required for federal grants. The issue stemmed from inconsistent processes and staff turnover, particularly at Metro Ride transit. No vendors were actually found to be debarred — the finding was procedural. The proposed policy amendment adds mandatory documentation steps, with additional technology fixes planned including a Workday workflow prompt and a SAM.gov API integration to auto-check vendors before payment. The committee approved the amendment unanimously with no significant debate.

discussions.item: Resolution of Public Depositories
discussions.body: This was a housekeeping item to update the resolution by removing former City Clerk Caitlyn and adding new City Clerk Rachel. The motion was approved unanimously without discussion.

discussions.item: Dog and Cat License Fee Increases
discussions.body: Staff proposed restoring the original 2026 fee increase proposal — raising the spayed/neutered dog/cat fee from $23 to $30 and reducing the microchip discount from $8 to $5, for a net fee of $25 — after the council had amended it last year. Chief Barnes explained the animal control fund has never been self-sustaining, with the cat contract with the Marathon County Humane Society costing $37,000 in 2025. Alder Tierney said she could not support such a large jump and suggested a $2–$3 increase instead. Alder Watson questioned whether Marathon County had yet set its own fees for the coming year, noting the city's action could be premature; staff confirmed they had not yet heard from the county. The committee agreed by consensus to postpone the item to the next meeting pending confirmation of Marathon County's fee schedule.

discussions.body: The committee briefly acknowledged this item in open session before moving to close session, as the real estate negotiation required confidential deliberation under Wisconsin State Statute 19.85(1)(e). overview: The Kronenwetter Plan Commission held its September 21, 2026 meeting with five of seven members present. The commission approved two significant items: a certified survey map adjusting a lot line on Wood Road/Tracy Court, and a conditional use permit for the Marathon County Highway Department garage. The Green Tree subdivision preliminary plat was discussed with no new action taken, as the matter has already been forwarded to the Village Board, and commissioners began preliminary discussion of a zoning ordinance review.

Guy Fridtelt of 2240 Ruby Drive argued that the proposed Green Tree subdivision is in a strategic location within the village's sewer service area and that approving private wells and septics there could block future municipal sewer and water extension to the east and south, citing the village's own comprehensive plan maps. He asked the commission to consult a civil engineer before proceeding. Bernie Kramer of 2150 East State Highway 153 expressed broader frustration with village leadership and economic development decisions, including the Marathon County Highway Department facility, calling it a 'total misfit' and criticizing a lack of accountability in local government. discussions.body: The chair noted the commission had resolved most issues at a prior meeting approximately a week and a half earlier and was down to one remaining issue: an agreement between Marathon County and Saint Ries Parish on seven listed items. discussions.body: The director provided an update noting the application was submitted June 11 and that the developer has agreed to an extension but state law presumes approval if the village board does not act within 90 days. He reported that the two previously flagged issues — stormwater management and emergency access via Nick Avenue — have been substantially addressed: stormwater details are underway, and a gated emergency access road with a Knox box will be built by the seller north of the centerline to preserve space near an existing residence. Developer representative Jill Schofield spoke, clarifying the history of the project including a prior higher-density proposal that was rejected, the engineering study of a lift station that was deemed cost-prohibitive, and the design of the emergency access. A commissioner noted that Roth Engineering had studied a connector to Tower subdivision but found a lift station would cost close to $1 million. title: Joint Board of Trustees and Finance and HR Committee Budget Workshop
overview: The Village of Weston held a joint budget workshop between the Board of Trustees and Finance and HR Committee to review the proposed 2027 budget, covering utility funds (water, sewer, stormwater) and the general fund. Key discussions centered on Mountain Bay Metro PD budget percentage calculations, employee wage structure and market positioning, and the utility rate outlook, with trustees and staff debating how to better compensate lower-paid employees. No final budget votes were taken; decisions on wages, the pay matrix, and borrowing were deferred to the October 5th meeting.

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: Two members of the public spoke. The first speaker, a woman identified as Grace, urged the board to think outside the box on wages, suggesting bonuses instead of across-the-board percentage raises to slow compensation growth for higher earners while accelerating pay for lower-paid employees. The second speaker, identified as living on 5000 Street Weston, raised multiple specific budget concerns: the Mountain Bay Metro PD budget showing a 3.09% increase versus the charter cap of 3% and the oversight board's approved 2.8%; the Everest Metro Municipal Court label on a $60,000 line item after that court's dissolution; a $0 allocation for building maintenance personnel despite $5,521 spent year-to-date; and criticism of the employee survey process, arguing full results were never presented to the board and that the board should set budget parameters and let department heads manage within them.

discussions.item: August 2026 Budget Status Report
discussions.body: The report was acknowledged by both the Finance and HR Committee and the Board of Trustees with no significant concerns raised. Finance Director Jessica noted that aquatic expenses would not be finalized until December due to pending water utility bills. A concern was raised about refuse/recycling fuel costs trending higher, with Jessica indicating the rate may need to increase to approximately $25 and that a formula and projection would be brought back to the board in October.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget - Water Utility Fund
discussions.body: Public Works Director Michael presented the water utility fund, noting Weston's water rates are on the lower end compared to neighboring communities. He reported the fund has positive net income currently, with a potential rate increase possible in the 2028-2029 timeframe if a major capital project is undertaken. Chemical costs have decreased by approximately $50,000 due to removing wells one and five from service. A spreadsheet typo was identified in the 2026 budget net assets beginning balance figure, which Jessica acknowledged needed correction. Ongoing PFAS settlement payments from 3M were confirmed as the source of miscellaneous revenue, with approximately five or six payments remaining.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget - Sanitary Sewer Utility Fund
discussions.body: Michael reported that Rim Mountain Metro Sanitary District is projecting approximately a $100,000 cost increase to Weston for 2027 due to a major wastewater treatment plant upgrade to meet phosphorus limits. He noted the sewer fund has been running at a deficit for several years, and the sale of the old sewervac truck helped close the gap in the current year, but no similar large asset exists for 2027. A sewer rate increase was identified as likely necessary in 2027. Weston's rates remain among the lower ones compared to other district partners including Kronenwetter, Rothschild, and Mosinee.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget - Stormwater Utility Fund
discussions.body: Michael described the stormwater utility, noting rates have been stable since a 2023 increase and the fund continues to show positive cash flow. A major upcoming project is the Business 51 storm pond, intended to improve compliance with DNR phosphorus requirements, with modeling showing 70-80% compliance achievement. Michael clarified that stormwater funds benefit rural areas through culvert projects, not just those with curb and gutter. Grant funding from DOT for the project and a pedestrian crossing has not yet been confirmed.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget - General Fund Revenues and Expenditures
discussions.body: Jessica presented the general fund, noting the state confirmed an allowable levy increase of $732,852 from TIF closure plus approximately $95,000 in additional operational levy capacity, for a total allowable operational levy of $6,601,041. A $54,822 decrease in the Expenditure Restraint Program aid was flagged because the village's tax rate approaching the $5 threshold resulted in a penalty-like reduction, while shared revenue increased by $52,494. The budget assumes a 3% across-the-board COLA wage increase and a 10% health insurance increase, with final health insurance figures expected September 30th. The mislabeling of the Everest Metro Municipal Court versus Rothschild Area Municipal Court was acknowledged and will be corrected.

discussions.item: Mountain Bay Metro PD Budget Percentage Debate
discussions.body: Trustees and staff engaged in extended discussion over why the Mountain Bay Metro PD budget line appeared to reflect a 3.09% increase when the charter caps increases at 3% and the oversight board approved 2.8%. Jessica explained that approximately $100,000 was moved to capital for police equipment, which skewed the percentage calculation on the remaining operating line, but the total dollar amount matched Mountain Bay's request. Trustees including Brent Olson and Barbara Ermeling expressed confusion and concern. The board directed staff to move all Mountain Bay Metro costs into the general fund operating line and shift equivalent borrowing to streets, and to reduce the capital allocation from $100,000 to $60,000 to match Mountain Bay's actual budgeted capital request, making the accounting cleaner and the percentage calculation accurate.

discussions.item: Employee Wages, Pay Matrix, and Market Positioning
discussions.body: Extensive discussion was held on employee compensation. Michael noted that 11 employees are between the midpoint and maximum of the pay matrix, and that no employee exceeds 104% of market rate. Staff and trustees discussed how annual COLA increases combined with annual matrix adjustments effectively move the finish line, making it difficult for lower-paid employees to reach the midpoint. Trustee Olson calculated that total personnel cost increases including 3% COLA, WRS, health insurance, $56,000 in public works market increases, and $15,000 in merit/market contingency totaled approximately $390,000, or roughly $9,027 per employee, prompting concern about sustainability. A trustee proposed applying a flat dollar amount rather than a flat percentage to each employee's midpoint so that lower-paid employees would receive a proportionally larger increase. Jessica and Michael agreed this concept would be brought back October 5th along with three formal motions: matrix percentage increase, salary COLA percentage, and merit/market contingency amount. Staff confirmed the $56,000 in public works market increases would be tied to GTA funds.

discussions.item: Employee Survey and Benefits Discussion
discussions.body: The board discussed results of an employee survey with a 62% participation rate (23 of 37 employees). Public comment had already raised concerns that full survey results were not presented to the board. Michael confirmed streets crews use 4-10 schedules in summer but utility staff found it logistically unworkable due to seven-day operational demands. The board reached informal consensus, with multiple trustees agreeing to discontinue considering summer hours or additional holidays and focus exclusively on financial compensation. A suggestion was made to revisit non-pay benefits on a periodic basis, perhaps every 18 months.

title: Executive Committee Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Executive Committee held a lengthy public meeting dominated by debate over the proposed Hub City Wind project by Alliant Energy. After 10 public commenters urged the committee to reject a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) with Alliant and instead pursue PSC intervention, the committee voted 8-2 to forward a resolution to the full County Board directing Alliant Energy to submit a proposed agreement addressing concerns raised by the alternative energy work group, with the agreement to be shared with affected townships upon receipt. The committee also received an update on the troubled Bug Tussle broadband project before moving into closed session.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Hub City Wind Project
discussions.body: Ten speakers signed up, with nearly all opposing a JDA with Alliant Energy and urging the county to instead pursue intervenor status at the PSC. Speakers including Tom Wilcox of Farmland First argued a county-level JDA risks preempting township zoning authority and asked the committee to join the townships' intergovernmental committee at the PSC. Joe Kiwok of the Town of Cleveland cited Columbia County's intervention as a model to follow. Mary Clues, speaking on behalf of the Marathon County Farmers Union, urged the county to negotiate hard rather than cede its power. Dean Beck warned against signing any NDA and urged baseline road assessments before construction. Glenn Regowski cited a Wausau Pilot poll showing the Hub City Wind Farm generated the strongest reader opposition of any poll, and noted he had seen no supporters from the five affected townships at any meeting.

discussions.body: Chair Gibbs called for approval of the minutes as presented in the packet. Supervisor Robinson moved and Supervisor Morash seconded. No discussion was held. The motion passed with an abstention granted to Supervisor Gao.

discussions.item: 2027 Annual Budget Development and Policy Recommendations
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard briefly noted that budget work is proceeding toward a September 29th presentation deadline, at which point the budget becomes the board's budget. Supervisor Robinson reminded all standing committees to weigh in at their September meetings, noting the Human Resource Finance Property Committee meets at 1:00 p.m. and the ERC at 3:00 p.m. on the 29th. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Discussion Regarding Request from Supervisor Endrris
discussions.body: Supervisor Mask questioned how Endrris contacted all his constituents given reports that his phone was out of service. Supervisor Boots disclosed that two AI detection tools rated the document 82–85% likely AI-generated, and he demonstrated by generating a counter-resolution using AI himself. Supervisor Robinson said regardless of authorship, the request raised real concerns but was 'overly broad' and potentially very expensive—estimating intervention costs at $50,000 to $200,000 or more depending on scope. Supervisor Gao recommended placing the request on file for now. No formal motion or vote was taken; the item was effectively deferred pending further scoping and cost analysis.

discussions.item: Consideration of Potential Engagement with Alliant Energy – Hub City Wind Project
discussions.body: CPZ staff presented a pros/cons matrix of four options: JDA negotiation (estimated up to $20,000), PSC intervention ($50,000–$200,000), moratorium (viewed as legally unenforceable for a 100+ MW project under Wis. Stat. 66.0401), and post-CPCN appeal. Staff noted the PSC could not recall any case where intervention stopped a wind project. Supervisor Robinson moved the 'Robinson resolution,' which directs Alliant Energy to submit a proposed agreement addressing work group concerns by November 1, 2025, with a further amendment added requiring the agreement be shared with governing bodies of affected townships upon receipt. Supervisor Gao proposed an alternative amendment drawing on the second resolution (putting negotiations on hold) but it was ruled out of order as it did not amend the Robinson resolution. Corporation Counsel clarified the committee's task was simply to forward a resolution to the full County Board, not to finalize county policy. The amendment to share the agreement with townships passed with one or more opposed; the full amended resolution passed 8-2 on a roll call vote.

discussions.item: Bug Tussle Broadband Update
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard summarized the history: a 2021 $25 million conduit financing for Bug Tussle Wireless to build a fiber ring around Marathon County, followed by a county-approved $8 million loan ($5M to complete the ring, $3M as match for a PSC broadband grant). The ring was never completed—only half was built due to cost overruns—and Bug Tussle has now requested an additional approximately $45 million from Marathon County as part of a $500 million ask across all participating counties for BEAD projects. Infrastructure committee received the Bug Tussle presentation September 3rd. The item was moved to closed session due to bargaining considerations and potential litigation.

One speaker's audio was partially cut in transcript. Common themes: distrust of Alliant Energy, opposition to a JDA, support for PSC intervention, concern about long-term land use and health impacts, and citing public survey results showing strong opposition to the project.

title: Board Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board of Supervisors met on September 17th and took action on multiple agenda items, most notably approving an amendment to Chapter 11.02 of the county's General Code of Ordinances updating the animal waste management ordinance after an extensive 18-month collaborative process with farmers and conservation groups. The board also approved numerous rezoning ordinances and postponed a vote on an infrastructure committee appointment after a supervisor raised concerns that the previous month's 'no' votes were based on 'sour grapes' rather than qualifications.

discussions.item: Public Comment: Animal Waste Ordinance
discussions.body: Seven of eight public speakers addressed the proposed animal waste ordinance amendment. Dairy farmers Kevin Schmiky (River Run Dairy, ~90 cows), Andrew Belter (~250 cows), Shannon Niclay (~300 cows, 2,100 acres), and Patrick Suchka (~400 acres) all expressed support, citing the value of nutrient management plans for farm finances and water quality. Michael Toris of the River Alliance of Wisconsin praised Marathon County as a statewide leader in collaborative watershed work. Tom Mueller of Miltrim Farms (~3,000 cows) supported the ordinance while stating it 'does not go far enough.' James Yetus spoke in opposition, calling the ordinance 'government overreach' and arguing that his 135-year farm operation should not be forced to adopt a nutrient management plan, and that the work group was stacked with supporters.

discussions.item: Public Comment: Town of Green Valley Rezoning
discussions.body: Mitch Maguire, speaking on behalf of the Town of Green Valley town board, argued that the board formally disapproved a rezoning of a parcel from urban agricultural zoning, that the county board must honor the town's statutory authority, and that the half-acre parcel was commercially used by a shoreline protection contractor (Lakeside Rip) and should be zoned commercial, not agricultural. Neighbor Rosley Maguire raised concerns about precedent, saying other residents had already expressed intent to rezone their own half-acre lots for storage if the petitioner's request was approved.

discussions.item: Infrastructure Committee Appointment (Item D14)
discussions.body: Supervisor Sybert addressed the item, reporting that after the previous month's 19-vote 'no' result, he called 15 of those 19 supervisors and 'not one of those 15 could say he wasn't qualified,' characterizing the opposition as 'sour grapes.' Sybert moved to postpone the vote until next month so supervisors could better evaluate the candidates. Supervisor Straw asked whether the infrastructure committee could function without a chair, and was told the vice chair would serve as acting chair and the committee could appoint an acting chair under Robert's Rules. The motion to postpone passed.

discussions.item: Town of Green Valley Sawyer Daget Rezoning (Ordinance 33-26, Item E16)
discussions.body: County land resources manager Shad Harvey explained that the 27-acre parcel is split-zoned and adjacent to general agricultural land, and that staff recommended rezoning to general agriculture to allow the property owner to build a large structure to store commercial equipment. Harvey clarified that the parcel is not a half-acre — it is 27 acres — and that the town's formal disapproval resolution did not meet statutory certification requirements. ERC voted unanimously to approve. Supervisor Ritter noted ERC considered sending it back to the town but both the petitioner and town representatives wanted a decision at the committee meeting. Supervisor Straw said he would vote against it out of deference to the town's position. Supervisor Morash noted that delay would leave the owner's equipment exposed outdoors over winter. The board approved the rezoning on a non-unanimous vote.

discussions.item: Animal Waste Ordinance Amendment (Chapter 11.02, Ordinance 41-26, Item E24)
discussions.body: County conservationist Kirsty Hidenrike and conservation analyst Matt Repang presented the ordinance, which was also reviewed by outside attorney Jane Landredy of Stafford Rosenbaum. Hidenrike described an 18-month process involving six public open houses, 13 ERC meetings, six farmer workgroup sessions, and 2,500 mailed notices. The ordinance targets winter spreading of liquid manure on frozen soils in February and March, requires nutrient management plans for relevant operations, and includes phased implementation timelines and emergency spreading provisions. Supervisor Sundowski asked detailed questions about which farms are covered, what monitoring is planned, and whether storm water from cities also contributes to algae blooms. Supervisor Morash raised concern about approving the ordinance without knowing the fee amount; Hidenrike explained that fees only apply to farms that winter-spread liquid manure and refuse to obtain a nutrient management plan, and that fee amounts would go through ERC and the county board before the 2028 implementation deadline. The amendment was approved.

discussions.item: DC Everest School District Facility Study (Educational Presentation)
discussions.body: DC Everest Superintendent Dr. Casey Nye and Director of Buildings and Grounds Jason Jablonski presented a two-year facility study driven by declining enrollment and an aging 75-year-old junior high building. The proposal involves decommissioning the junior high, redistributing grades to existing buildings, adding bus drop-off improvements at Mountain Bay Middle School, and adding a wing at the senior high. Enrollment has dropped from approximately 6,000 to 5,700 students with incoming classes of 300-350 versus graduating classes of 450. Dr. Nye said the projects could be completed with no additional tax impact if a pool renovation is excluded. Board Chair Gibbs asked about long-term enrollment trajectory. Nye noted a junior high walkthrough is scheduled for October 6th for interested supervisors.

publicComment: Eight speakers signed up for public comment. Seven spoke on the animal waste ordinance: dairy farmers Kevin Schmiky, Andrew Belter, Shannon Niclay, and Patrick Suchka all expressed support, citing the collaborative process and financial and environmental benefits of nutrient management plans. Michael Toris of the River Alliance of Wisconsin praised Marathon County's watershed collaboration. Tom Mueller of Miltrim Farms (3,000 cows) supported the ordinance but said it did not go far enough. James Yetus of the town of Easton spoke in opposition, calling it government overreach and arguing the workgroup was not representative of opponents. Two speakers — Mitch Maguire and Rosley Maguire — spoke on the Town of Green Valley rezoning, urging the board to honor the town's formal disapproval and warning of precedent-setting risk if agricultural zoning is applied to a commercial contractor's parcel.

overview: The DC Everest School Board held its September 2026 regular meeting, approving a 19.1% health insurance premium increase with Aspirus Health Plan for the 2027 plan year and receiving updates on the planned relocation of the IDEA and Odyssey alternative schools as part of an ongoing district facility consolidation effort driven by declining enrollment. The board also heard reports on teacher hiring trends, summer professional development, and community economic impact from the GTCC facility before adjourning to closed session to discuss seclusion and restraint matters.

discussions.item: WASB Legislative Update and Statewide Referendum Landscape
discussions.body: Grabko reported that the WASB September update noted 71 Wisconsin school districts will have 78 referendum questions on the November ballot, bringing the 2026 statewide total to 154 questions across 145 districts — down from a record 241 in 2024. She noted this context was relevant given DC Everest's ongoing facility study and community survey. WASB's four legislative priorities for the 2027-29 budget cycle were also outlined, including increasing special education categorical aid and providing inflationary increases to spendable resources.

discussions.item: Student Representative Report
discussions.body: New student council president Bin Campman, a senior at DC Everest Senior High, reported on the school year's start including a sophomore orientation assembly, homecoming plans with a board games theme, and strong athletic results. Notable highlights included the girls tennis team's 14-3 record and a 5-0 sweep, boys soccer wins including a 'Derby' rivalry victory over Wausau West, and the first-ever inclusion of freshmen in homecoming activities such as powderpuff and hallway decorating.

discussions.item: Superintendent Report
discussions.body: Superintendent Dr. Nye discussed several topics: implementation of Wisconsin Act 89 tightening adult-student communication expectations; DC Everest's participation in the national Brightspots cohort with a site visit to Rothschild Elementary highlighted; launch of the community-wide facility survey running through October 9th; GTCC being fully booked every weekend for the coming year with the World Horseshoe Tournament generating an estimated $5.1 million total economic impact this summer; and a potential social media class action lawsuit that the district has been invited to join, which Nye said would be discussed in closed session next month. He also announced Rachel Rentmester as the incoming executive assistant, succeeding the retiring Ellen.

discussions.item: IDEA and Odyssey Relocation Update
discussions.body: Dr. Lindell presented plans to relocate both alternative schools from their current shared building, citing declining enrollment creating feasibility for decommissioning the facility. IDEA, which transitioned from a charter school to a district program in April, is planned to move to the high school campus footprint for the next school year, enabling students greater access to senior high courses. Odyssey is planned to relocate to the 'blue wing' of Evergreen Elementary, with a separate entrance maintained. Board members asked about parent concerns; Lindell and Dr. Nye acknowledged difficult community conversations, noting parents are particularly concerned about the loss of dedicated square footage, and that fundraising suggestions were raised but cannot resolve the underlying staffing cost issues from declining enrollment. Current enrollment caps are 72 students per school; IDEA is in the upper 60s and Odyssey is also in the upper 60s.

discussions.item: Mission Moment: Rothschild Raptor Mural
discussions.body: Principal Mr. Alexen presented the completed Rothschild Raptor mural installed in August on the school's gymnasium stage. The project was funded through community partnerships including People's State Bank, the DC Everest Foundation, Clover Belt Credit Union, Brokaw Credit Union, and others. The mural features a raptor alongside imagery of Rib Mountain, Lake Wausau, and the local landscape, and was designed by local muralist Jessica Copeki. Alexen noted the school's theme this year is 'Raptor Nation.'

discussions.item: Health Insurance Renewal - Aspirus Health Plan
discussions.body: Dr. Nye presented the recommended renewal with Aspirus Health Plan for the 2027 plan year, noting an initial proposed increase of 44% was negotiated down to 31% and ultimately to 19.1% with plan design changes including increased deductibles and co-insurance. The district will maintain a 0% premium option for full-time employees, add employer HSA contributions of $1,000 single/$2,000 family, and cap part-time employee premium contributions at 30% for family coverage. Nye estimated approximately 75% of staff would not see an increase in out-of-pocket costs based on historical claims. The board approved the renewal without discussion.

discussions.item: General Annual Hiring Report
discussions.body: HR Director Sarah presented the hiring report, noting 28 teacher hires this year consistent with 29 last year, with 71% having five or fewer years of experience and 40% previously connected to DC Everest. The teacher candidate pool has rebounded to pre-COVID levels. Support staff openings dropped from 17 to 11 since the report was compiled. Board members including Yee Leng Xiong, Larry Schaefer, and Lindsey Lewitzke asked about geographic origins of hires, retention of early-career teachers, and what board policies contribute to successful hiring. Schaefer raised concerns about the well-documented pattern of losing teachers with under five years of experience. Special education was identified as the greatest area of ongoing hiring need.

discussions.item: Summer Professional Development Update
discussions.body: Dr. Lindell reported over 2,100 hours of professional development completed over the summer, with a focus on PLC work, academic clarity, and responsive classroom training. Over 50 staff attended responsive classroom training funded by grants, with Rothschild Elementary serving as the pilot school. Lindell noted teachers are reporting this as among the best starts to a school year they can remember, with staff physically tired but not emotionally depleted — a meaningful shift in teacher experience.

discussions.body: The board voted unanimously to adjourn to closed session pursuant to Wisconsin State Statute 19.85(1)(f) to discuss seclusion and restraint matters involving specific persons whose personal or disciplinary data, if discussed publicly, could adversely affect their reputation.

title: Administrative Policy Committee Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Administrative Policy Committee met on September 15, 2026, focusing primarily on a lengthy finance director update covering the 2027 budget process, debt restructuring, staffing concerns, garbage fee increases driven by diesel surcharges, and the 10-year Capital Improvement Plan. No formal votes were taken; the meeting was largely a working session to prepare trustees for October budget workshops. Key issues included a $54,000 unplanned fuel surcharge cost from Harter's garbage contract, a proposed restructuring of $863,200 in unspent TID 2 borrowing proceeds, and concerns about understaffing across village departments.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Traffic on Old Highway 51 and Long-Range Planning
discussions.body: Bernie Kramer of 2150 East State Highway 153 addressed the committee, raising concerns about traffic management on Old Highway 51, arguing it is Kronenwetter's responsibility to coordinate with the county on traffic improvements rather than remaining passive. He also expressed skepticism about 10-year planning given how frequently elected boards change. An unidentified trustee noted she had spoken with Kramer earlier and agreed his suggestion about a potential turning lane for heavy equipment was worth considering.

discussions.item: Finance Director Report - Staffing and Operational Concerns
discussions.body: Finance Director John Jacobs provided an extensive update covering the financial audit (targeting mid-October), TID 3 closure audit (joint review board planned for November), property reassessment by Associated Appraisal (fieldwork underway on 3,000 parcels with buildings and 4,400 land parcels), and a potential future RFP for auditing services. Village Administrator Jim [last name inaudible] and Jacobs both emphasized the village is severely understaffed, with Jacobs noting there were days he was the only person in the office. Discussion centered on the need for a deputy finance director and the strain on interim clerk Kim, who is also managing election duties.

discussions.item: Garbage Fee - Diesel Fuel Surcharge
discussions.body: Jacobs presented a handout analyzing the impact of diesel fuel prices exceeding $4 per gallon — the threshold triggering a fuel surcharge clause in the Harter's garbage contract. Since March 2026, diesel has exceeded $4 (reaching over $6 per gallon), creating approximately $54,000 in unplanned costs for 2026, which the village plans to absorb using the $60,000 contingency reserve and $43,000 from TID 3 closure revenue. For the 2027 budget, trustees discussed three diesel price scenarios ($5.75, $6.00, $6.25 per gallon) that would add $28–$30 per household to garbage charges on top of the contract's standard 4% increase. Trustees agreed to plan for the worst-case $6.25 scenario, adding approximately $30 to the rate.

discussions.item: 2027 Operating Budget Preview
discussions.body: Jacobs and the administrator outlined anticipated 2027 budget additions: a deputy clerk position (funded 100% by general fund), a possible fourth utility crew member (funded by water/sewer rates), and retention of funding for the planning tech position. Police officers union contract negotiations are ongoing for a proposed three-year contract; a first bargaining session with the teamsters is scheduled for September 24. The state-mandated levy limit increase for 2027 is only $16,306, well short of anticipated cost increases, meaning the village will again need to use the general obligation debt service exception — similar to the $874,000 exception used in 2026.

discussions.item: 2027-2036 CIP Budget - Debt Restructuring
discussions.body: Jacobs detailed a proposed restructuring of $863,200 in unspent TID 2 borrowing proceeds that cannot be used for TID 2 projects (the Flannery Jamrose project was scrapped after bids came in over $1.2 million). The funds must be spent by late 2027 and will be transferred to the village's general capital project fund, with the associated debt absorbed by the tax levy debt service fund. This eliminates one of two previously anticipated debt service 'drops' — the 2030 drop — while preserving the 2029 drop of approximately $226,000. Jacobs noted the restructuring may allow TID 2 to close a year or two earlier than scheduled. Budget workshops are scheduled for October 13 (full budget review at 5:30 p.m.), October 19 (3:00 p.m. start to accommodate Plan Commission at 6:00 p.m.), and October 20 (6:00 p.m.).

discussions.item: Future Agenda Items - Committee Ordinance and Public Comment Policy
discussions.body: The administrator noted that Village President Dan Joling had referenced a potential ordinance change at the prior village board meeting to allow a member of the Police and Fire Commission to simultaneously serve on another committee — currently prohibited by ordinance. The administrator said the matter will go to the village attorney before coming to APC. Trustee Mary Solheim raised the topic of revising public comment procedures at APC, and the administrator indicated a recommendation will be brought forward, noting that allowing emailed public comment on non-agenda items is unusual statewide and has created problems.

publicComment: One speaker appeared in person: Bernie Kramer, 2150 East State Highway 153, Kronenwetter. Kramer expressed skepticism about long-range 10-year planning given board turnover, and criticized village inaction on Old Highway 51 traffic issues, arguing Kronenwetter bears responsibility for working with the county to address traffic concerns — particularly as heavy commercial development increases. He urged the village to take the first step in coordinating with Marathon County rather than treating Old 51 as someone else's problem.

title: Town Hall Meeting: Overview of Professional City Management Models
overview: The City of Wausau held a public town hall meeting to educate residents and council members about professional city management models, specifically the city administrator and city manager forms of government. Dr. Michael Ford of UW-Oshkosh and Jay Shambo, a current interim city administrator, presented information on governance structures, fiscal data, and practical experience. No votes were taken; the meeting was informational only, though Mayor Doug Diny indicated the city is actively exploring hiring a city administrator and looking at including funding in the budget, potentially phasing in as early as mid-2027.

agenda.item: Welcome and introduction by Mayor Doug Diny
Introduction of Dr. Michael Ford and Jay Shambo
Dr. Ford presentation: Logic of professional local management
